papers.title: How Will the 340B Rebate Model Pilot Affect Covered Entity Finances?
papers.abstract: The Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) plans to implement a pilot switching 340B from an upfront discount model to a rebate model for drugs in the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program (MDPNP). This study uses calibration methods to predict the impact of the rebate model pilot (RMP) on covered entities’ net revenues from the 340B program. I examine possible losses from averted duplicate discounts; denial of valid claims; manufacturers using data to exert influence; liquidity-related expenses; and administrative and staffing costs. I also project the effects of switching the entire 340B program to a rebate model. I project net revenue losses from the RMP of $1.5 billion. Expansion to all of 340B would increase the predicted losses to $22.8 billion, cutting net revenues from the program by 32%. The majority of losses will come from administrative and staffing costs, which do not benefit manufacturers, implying a net negative effect of switching to a rebate model. Covered entity losses from the RMP will be limited by the pilot only applying to a small percentage of 340B sales as well as restrictions HRSA’s guidance places on manufacturers. If the rebate model expands to all of 340B or if the restrictions are inadequately enforced, the losses will grow substantially.

papers.title: Horizontal Equity of Taxation: Citizen Beliefs and Policy Preferences
papers.abstract: Taxes are harder to enforce on the self-employed than on wage earners, creating horizontal inequities among taxpayers with similar incomes. Using tax microsimulation and household survey data from 29 developing countries, we show that horizontal inequities in actual tax systems are comparable in magnitude to vertical equity and are exacerbated by progressive reforms that fall disproportionately on wage earners. We then conduct surveys and randomized information experiments in Pakistan to study public perceptions of these inequities. Although providing information raises fairness concerns, it does not increase support for reforms reducing it, revealing an important political constraint to improving tax equity.

papers.title: Decoding Success: Phonics-based Instruction and Student Achievement
papers.abstract: Reading is a foundational skill, yet fewer than one in three US fourth graders read at a proficient level. How best to teach reading and improve educational attainment has been an active policy debate for decades. Recently, phonics-based approaches have surged in popularity, even though the largest attempt to put similar methods into classrooms was previously abandoned out of concerns that the program was ineffective. This paper studies Reading First, a nearly $1 billion per year federal program established under No Child Left Behind that promoted phonics-based instruction in K-3 classrooms. Exploiting administrative data from Texas and program eligibility formulas, we estimate effects via difference-in-differences and instrumental variables specifications. We find that eligibility increased third-grade reading test scores by 0.1 standard deviations and that effects persisted through at least the eighth grade. An analysis of digitized exam questions shows that treated students outperformed peers on questions that required basic decoding skills and those with more words, a benefit that also drove improvements in math scores. We follow exposed cohorts into early adulthood, finding that the program increased on-time high school graduation, college enrollment, four-year college completion, and adult earnings at age 25.

papers.title: The Last Arbitrage? Capital Flows, Development, and Infrastructure as an Asset Class
papers.abstract: Lucas (1990) asked why capital does not flow from rich to poor countries. When poor countries opened their stock markets to foreign investors in the late 1980s, it did: rich-country capital arbitraged away the excess return on emerging-market equity and created a new asset class. Infrastructure may offer the last such arbitrage. The median social return on paved roads in poor countries was 3.7 times the return on U.S. capital at the time of liberalization, but investors capture only the share of social returns that contracts, user fees, and political risk allow, a constraint we call the private foreign hurdle. Confidential IFC data show that its infrastructure equity portfolio outperformed the S&P 500 by 2 percentage points per year, even though only 41 percent of individual investments in the portfolio did so. This suggests that strong risk-adjusted portfolio returns can mask substantial project-specific uncertainty. Despite high social returns, transportation accounted for just 9 IFC infrastructure project investments versus 157 in power and telecommunications. This raises the question of whether private investors can appropriate enough of the social returns on infrastructure to make these investments. Moreover, investors cannot learn from returns they cannot see. Disclosure of historical equity returns is therefore necessary, but not sufficient, to efficiently mobilize more private capital for infrastructure. Because the benefits of disclosure accrue to the market, not to any one firm, multilateral development banks, working with an independent research partner, are best placed to provide it.

papers.title: The Role of Parental Beliefs and Public Policies in Financing Higher Education: An Experimental Study
papers.abstract: Parents who want to financially support their child’s pursuit of higher education must save against assumptions about what college will cost and how it will be funded. This study examines how parental beliefs and future borrowing costs shape college saving decisions. Through a survey experiment with an embedded financial planning tool, we elicit parental beliefs about the future costs of college and their expectations of different funding sources, including financial aid and student loans. We find that nearly all parents want to cover some of the future costs of college, but many may fall short in their savings due to underestimating future expenses and overestimating available financial aid. A corrective information intervention encourages most parents to recalibrate their saving target. However, when a substantial gap between expected and actual costs is combined with a salient high repayment burden for their child, we find a discouragement effect that diminishes both their willingness to save and their aspirations for their child’s educational attainment. We calibrate a model of parental saving with learning about college costs, which reproduces both the absence of an average response to borrowing costs and the shift of children away from college attendance, and use it to price the welfare cost of misperception. Parents with higher financial literacy hold better-calibrated beliefs and respond more to correction. We discuss policy implications for outreach activities to support informed financial planning for college education.

papers.title: The Recent and Impending Evolution of US Federal Support for State and Local Governments
papers.abstract: In the US federal system, the federal government provides substantial fiscal support to state and local governments. In this paper, we describe how the landscape of intergovernmental grants, which exceeded $1.2 trillion in 2025, evolved during and in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. We provide short-run evidence on how state and local government budgets have adapted as pandemic-era fiscal supports wound down. We further emphasize the pressures state and local budgets will face as several provisions of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), which are intended to restrain intergovernmental grants, go into effect over the coming years.
